source_caption:
There are two different groups of candidates for the role of Mia Wallace in 𝐏𝐮𝐥𝐩 𝐅𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: actresses who appeared on Quentin Tarantino’s original casting wish list, and actresses who were reportedly considered/interviewed later by Tarantino or Miramax.⁣
⁣
For Mia Wallace, the names reported across the strongest sources include:⁣
⁣
• Uma Thurman (eventually cast⁣)
• Michelle Pfeiffer (reportedly Tarantino’s preferred alternative)
• Meg Ryan⁣
• Holly Hunter⁣
• Rosanna Arquette⁣
• Isabella Rossellini⁣
• Halle Berry⁣
• Julia Louis-Dreyfus⁣
• Virginia Madsen⁣
• Patricia Arquette⁣
• Jennifer Beals⁣
• Pam Grier⁣
• Bridget Fonda⁣
• Robin Wright⁣
• Meg Tilly⁣
• Madonna⁣
⁣
The interesting part is that Uma Thurman wasn’t actually on Tarantino’s surviving original typed wish list. As the casting process continued, however, Thurman emerged as a serious possibility, and Tarantino quickly became convinced that she was the right actress for Mia Wallace.⁣
⁣
Thurman herself was not immediately convinced that she wanted the role. At the time, she was in her early twenties and had already appeared in films such as Dangerous Liaisons, but parts of the Pulp Fiction screenplay left her unsure about accepting it.⁣
⁣
Tarantino, however, was determined to convince her. According to Thurman, he called her and spent a long time discussing the film and the character. He even read parts of the script to her over the phone. His enthusiasm eventually changed her mind.

source_details.title: Pulp Fiction
source_details.synopsis: Pulp Fiction is a 1994 American crime film written and directed by Quentin Tarantino from a story he conceived with Roger Avary. It tells four intertwining tales of crime and violence in Los Angeles. The film stars John Travolta, Samuel L. Jackson, Bruce Willis, Tim Roth, Ving Rhames, and Uma Thurman. The title refers to the pulp magazines and hardboiled crime novels popular during the mid-twentieth century, known for their graphic violence and punchy dialogue. Tarantino wrote Pulp Fiction in 1992 and 1993, incorporating scenes that Avary originally wrote for True Romance (1993). Its plot occurs out of chronological order.
